title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
pattern: DP: best subsequence ending at each index
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest **strictly increasing subsequence**. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements.

example.why: For example 1, 4, 5 (or 3, 4, 5, or 1, 2, 5). No increasing subsequence has four elements.

idea: Let `dp[i]` be the length of the longest increasing subsequence that **ends exactly at index i**. Alone, every element is a subsequence of length 1.
The element before `nums[i]` in such a subsequence must be an earlier, **smaller** number `nums[j]`. Then `nums[i]` extends the best subsequence ending at `j`: length `dp[j] + 1`.
Try every earlier `j` and keep the best. The answer is the largest value in `dp` — the subsequence may end anywhere.

complexity.timeWhy: Every pair (j, i) is compared once. (A patience-sorting variant with binary search reaches O(n log n).)

steps.text: Our example: **`nums = [3,1,4,2,5]`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Every number on its own is an increasing subsequence of length 1, so every `dp[i]` starts at 1.
